title: The Tuxedo Begins

jokes.text: Fifth Avenue is closed for a joint pain walkathon. It's only four blocks but they are so slow.
jokes.setup: Jack explains why he's late — a walkathon closed the street
jokes.punchline: The walkathon is for joint pain sufferers, so the participants move agonizingly slowly, making traffic worse than it would be otherwise
jokes.explanation: Tight, well-constructed joke. The specificity of 'joint pain' walkathon creating an ironic traffic jam is clever. Economy is excellent — two sentences, full payoff. Not quite legendary but genuinely sharp writing.

jokes.text: My subway ride was the standard amazingness. No, that's not how it works. Let people off first, otherwise... The train's going express for no reason.
jokes.setup: Liz says her subway ride was 'standard amazingness'
jokes.punchline: She immediately contradicts herself by listing all the infuriating things that happened — people blocking the door, express trains with no warning
jokes.explanation: The sarcastic opener 'standard amazingness' is a strong character beat for Liz — relatable frustration delivered with her specific brand of aggrieved competence. The list of subway sins is universally recognizable.

jokes.text: Next stop, one millionth street and Central Park jogger memorial highway.
jokes.setup: Liz is ranting about the subway going express with no reason
jokes.punchline: The absurd stop name — 'one millionth street' suggests the train has gone impossibly far, compounded by naming a highway after a famous violent crime
jokes.explanation: Two-part absurdist joke packed into one line. 'One millionth street' is a funny exaggeration of how far express trains skip; naming the highway after the Central Park Jogger case is darkly subversive. The compression is impressive.

jokes.text: Am I the last one in this city still following the rules of being a person?
jokes.setup: Liz has endured subway rudeness and walkathon-caused traffic
jokes.punchline: The grandiose phrasing 'rules of being a person' for mundane subway etiquette captures Liz's self-righteous exasperation perfectly
jokes.explanation: Highly character-specific. Liz's martyrdom complex delivered as a sincere question is very on-brand. The phrase 'rules of being a person' is quotable and captures her worldview economically.

jokes.text: # Three bucks, two bags, one me #
jokes.setup: Liz declares New York is overrated and storms off
jokes.punchline: She punctuates her exit by singing a jingle — a parody of Jay-Z's 'Empire State of Mind' hook but about her sad, budget-conscious existence
jokes.explanation: Brilliantly economic. The callback to Jay-Z's 'Empire State of Mind' structure ('concrete jungle where dreams are made of') but reduced to 'three bucks, two bags, one me' perfectly encapsulates Liz's unglamorous New York experience. Extremely character-integrated — this could only be Liz.

jokes.text: Say, where does a young prostitute get started in this town?
jokes.setup: Liz and Jack are debating whether New York is great or overrated on a city street
jokes.punchline: A random passerby interjects with an absurdly inappropriate question as if joining a normal conversation, undercutting Jack's romantic view of New York
jokes.explanation: Perfect comic timing — lands right as Jack is about to defend New York's greatness. The question is so specifically absurd ('young prostitute,' politely phrased) that it becomes a perfect illustration of Liz's point without belaboring it.

jokes.text: Lemon, we live in the world capital of culture, finance and King Kong attacks.
jokes.setup: Jack is defending New York as the greatest city in the world
jokes.punchline: He lists legitimate civic achievements then drops 'King Kong attacks' as if it's equally valid and prestigious
jokes.explanation: Excellent rule-of-three with a perfect absurdist pivot. Jack's pompous delivery makes the non-sequitur land harder. 'King Kong attacks' is specific enough to be funny as a civic boast — it implies New York is so great even giant apes come for it. Very quotable.

jokes.text: I quote, 'she is a thug in a cocktail dress.' Alex McCord, Real Housewives of New York.
jokes.setup: Liz argues New York is a testament to man's selfishness
jokes.punchline: She cites a Real Housewives quote as authoritative cultural commentary, treating reality TV as intellectual source material
jokes.explanation: Good character moment — Liz deploying Real Housewives as serious citation is very her. The specificity of the attribution (Alex McCord about Luann) rewards fans of both shows.

jokes.text: Give me your wallet. Now, technically that was about Luann being a bitch at Sonja's art show.
jokes.setup: Liz's Real Housewives quote is interrupted mid-sentence by what sounds like a mugger demanding a wallet
jokes.punchline: She immediately clarifies that the quote was contextualized differently — the 'give me your wallet' appears to be an actual mugging or street interruption, then she pivots back to RHONY analysis
jokes.explanation: Excellent structural joke — the mugging line lands as ambient New York chaos (proving Liz's point), then the pivot back to RHONY minutiae shows Liz's priorities. The transition is seamless and rewards attention.

jokes.text: But hey, you never let me talk about h-wives this long.
jokes.setup: Jack is distracted/compliant after the mugging interruption
jokes.punchline: Liz's self-aware aside reveals she's been monitoring Jack's tolerance for Real Housewives talk and notices he's unusually permissive — she's delighted by the anomaly
jokes.explanation: Solid character beat that establishes the Jack/Liz dynamic economically. 'H-wives' is a funny contraction. Not exceptional but functional relationship comedy.

jokes.text: I don't know if Sonja's ever gonna finish that toaster oven cookbook, but if she does, I am gonna buy it.
jokes.setup: Jack tries to redirect; Liz is in rare territory of being allowed to talk about Real Housewives
jokes.punchline: She uses her extra airtime not for something important but to share a sincere, trivial opinion about a reality TV star's cookbook project
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'toaster oven cookbook' is funny on its own. Liz's genuine investment in this minor celebrity's creative project is perfectly in character. Good lowkey delivery joke.

jokes.text: Ugh, I can actually feel myself getting sick. Am I the only person who saw Obama's press conference on how to sneeze?
jokes.setup: Liz is getting sick, surrounded by presumably germ-spreading New Yorkers
jokes.punchline: She implies there was a presidential press conference specifically dedicated to sneeze technique, and that only she paid attention — her rule-following martyrdom applied to public health
jokes.explanation: Very Liz — she watched Obama's H1N1-era public health guidance and took it as gospel while being appalled no one else did. 'Press conference on how to sneeze' is a funny reduction of public health theater.

jokes.text: Oh, what is that smell?! The gym said the odor was attracting bugs that were attracting bats that were attracting bat-hawks.
jokes.setup: Kenneth delivers Liz's gym bag; someone reacts to the smell
jokes.punchline: The escalating ecological chain reaction from gym smell → bugs → bats → bat-hawks (a made-up apex predator) is absurdist escalation comedy at its finest
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional. The escalation is perfectly structured: each step is logical given the previous one, but 'bat-hawks' as a newly-coined species is a brilliant invention. The show earns the absurdism by committing to the chain of causation. 'Bat-hawks' alone is a quotable coinage. This is among the episode's best jokes.

jokes.text: Unlike the d-bag who let the elevator door close on me this morning. It was funny because you were so mad.
jokes.setup: Liz says she cares how her behavior affects people, unlike others
jokes.punchline: Jack immediately reveals he was the elevator d-bag and found her anger amusing — the person she's complaining about is standing right there
jokes.explanation: Classic sitcom structure executed well. Jack's total lack of remorse ('it was funny because you were so mad') is perfectly in character — he's not apologetic, he's amused. The economy is tight.

jokes.text: Boy, when I move on to my new job I'm sure gonna miss you two and your whole Sam and Diane thing.
jokes.setup: Pete observes Jack and Liz bickering
jokes.punchline: He compares their dynamic to Sam and Diane from Cheers — a classic will-they-won't-they antagonistic relationship — while announcing he's leaving, which deflates any warmth
jokes.explanation: The Cheers reference works as a self-aware meta-comment on the Jack/Liz dynamic. Pete's casual mention of 'my new job' is a good secondary joke. Competent but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Uh, Sam and Diane are the lesbian couple in my building who murdered each other.
jokes.setup: Pete makes a Cheers reference assuming Liz will understand it
jokes.punchline: Liz completely misunderstands, thinking Pete is referring to real neighbors — and casually mentions they 'murdered each other' as an afterthought
jokes.explanation: Exceptional joke. The misdirection works on two levels: Liz's pop culture obliviousness (she doesn't recognize Cheers) AND the dark absurdism of 'murdered each other' delivered as casual neighbor gossip. The construction is tight — every word earns its place. 'Who murdered each other' as a throwaway clause is classic 30 Rock dark comedy.

jokes.text: It's in my contract that I only play blondes, non-Irish redheads, or bald sex robots.
jokes.setup: Jenna objects to wearing a costume for a commercial parody
jokes.punchline: Her contractual hair-color rider is specific enough to feel real but includes 'bald sex robots' as a legitimate acting category
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. The three-part list escalates perfectly: two normal(ish) categories then 'bald sex robots' as if it's a standard SAG distinction. Character integration is near-perfect — only Jenna would have this rider and only Jenna would cite it seriously. Extremely quotable.

jokes.text: Well then have Liz do it. She already has the frown lines. There, there they are.
jokes.setup: Jenna suggests Liz play the 'old lady before picture' because she looks old enough
jokes.punchline: Liz's reaction (presumably a scowl or frown) physically confirms Jenna's point in real time — 'there they are' suggests Liz's defensive reaction deepens the frown lines being referenced
jokes.explanation: The two-beat structure is well-executed. First the insult, then Jenna watches Liz's face react and the reaction proves the insult. 'There, there they are' is a great callback within the same joke — tight writing.

jokes.text: As always, I will step up and help because without people like me, civil society collapses completely.
jokes.setup: Jenna refuses the old lady costume; Liz reluctantly agrees to wear it
jokes.punchline: Liz frames agreeing to wear an unflattering costume as an act of profound civic virtue — her martyrdom complex inflated to absurd proportions
jokes.explanation: Strong character comedy. The gap between the stakes (wearing a wig for a TV bit) and Liz's self-importance ('civil society collapses') is perfectly calibrated. This is core Liz Lemon characterization.

jokes.text: Oh, don't be so dramatic. That's my thing. And if you take it away from me, I will kill myself. And then you.
jokes.setup: Liz's dramatic proclamation about civil society collapsing
jokes.punchline: Jenna calls her out for being dramatic — then immediately demonstrates far greater dramatic excess with a death threat, entirely unaware of the irony
jokes.explanation: Near-perfect joke. Three-beat structure: accusation → escalation to murder → casual addition of 'and then you.' The irony is completely earned (Jenna has NO self-awareness), the dark escalation lands because the character is established. 'And then you' as a two-word afterthought is a masterclass in comic economy. This is among the episode's very best jokes.

jokes.text: I won an Oscar, so now I get to do real art. Begins no dogs phase.
jokes.setup: Tracy announces his artistic evolution following his Oscar win
jokes.punchline: 'Begins no dogs phase' is delivered as if it's a coherent artistic statement — Tracy declaring a moratorium on dogs as part of his artistic maturity
jokes.explanation: Excellent Tracy absurdism. 'Begins no dogs phase' parodies the pretentious artist's 'period' language (blue period, etc.) but applied to Tracy's inscrutable logic. The economy is superb — four words carry enormous comedic weight.

jokes.text: This lamp is you. Ow, hot!
jokes.setup: Jack tries to hug Liz but she warns him she's sick; he substitutes a lamp for her
jokes.punchline: He immediately burns himself on the lamp — the physical gag undercuts his stoic professionalism with immediate physical consequence
jokes.explanation: Simple but effective physical comedy. The lamp-as-Liz-substitute is a sweet character moment; the immediate 'Ow, hot!' deflates it perfectly. Economy is excellent.

jokes.text: How black was this dude? On a scale from Lisa Bonet to Dotcom.
jokes.setup: The team discusses Jack's mugger
jokes.punchline: Tracy creates his own racial spectrum scale using two specific cultural references — Lisa Bonet (lighter-skinned) to Dotcom (his very dark-skinned associate) — delivered with complete earnestness
jokes.explanation: Very Tracy — he creates his own taxonomic system for a question that doesn't need one. The use of real people (Lisa Bonet) alongside his own character (Dotcom) as anchors for the spectrum is bold and specific. The earnestness sells it.

jokes.text: My assailant was a middle-aged white man wearing a button down shirt and Dockers. Dockers! Not some drug addict or gang aficionado. His knife was from Eddie Bauer.
jokes.setup: The gang expects a stereotypical mugger description; Jack reveals it was a mundane middle-class man
jokes.punchline: The horror is entirely in the brand specificity — Dockers and Eddie Bauer knife as symbols of normalized desperation. Jack's repetition of 'Dockers!' as an expletive is perfect.
jokes.explanation: Excellent social comedy. The joke works on multiple levels: parody of Jack's class-based assumptions, genuine social commentary about economic desperation, and the comic absurdity of 'Eddie Bauer knife' as a specific detail. 'Gang aficionado' is a perfect Jackism. The repetition of 'Dockers!' as if it's the most shocking word in the English language is brilliant.

jokes.text: Please interrupt me. This is a sign. The lower classes are getting cranky about the rich earning all of their money away from them. Can't they see this is in their best interest? How could we pay their salaries without using their money?
jokes.setup: Jack is about to deliver a pompous analysis of class warfare
jokes.punchline: 'Please interrupt me' is a rare moment of self-awareness immediately abandoned; 'earning all of their money away from them' is a masterful euphemism for wealth extraction; the circular logic about salaries is devastating satire
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's strongest jokes. 'Earning all of their money away from them' is a genuinely brilliant piece of writing — it captures trickle-down ideology's internal logic in one phrase. 'Please interrupt me' then abandoning the self-awareness is perfect Jack characterization. This works as satire AND character comedy simultaneously.

jokes.text: It's Ghostbusters 2 all over again.
jokes.setup: Jack and Liz debate whether the mugging signals a class war or just New York being New York
jokes.punchline: Liz compares the situation to Ghostbusters 2 — a movie about collective negativity making a villain stronger — which is both an apt and hilariously reductive cultural reference for a class warfare discussion
jokes.explanation: Good cultural reference joke that actually makes thematic sense — Ghostbusters 2's villain feeds on negativity, mirroring Liz's argument that New York's selfishness compounds itself. Not random name-dropping; it's earned.

jokes.text: It's the original Ghostbusters all over again.
jokes.setup: Liz said the situation was 'Ghostbusters 2 all over again'
jokes.punchline: Jack insists it's the original — meaning his interpretation (heroic response) is better than Liz's (despair) — the debate about New York's soul is argued entirely in Ghostbusters franchise terms
jokes.explanation: The callback is perfectly timed and adds a new dimension — the entire Jack/Liz philosophical debate is now a Ghostbusters quality argument. Jack choosing the original over the sequel as a metaphor for his optimism vs. Liz's pessimism is a clever layering. The economy is perfect — four words do enormous work.

jokes.text: 'Concrete bunghole where dreams are made up. There's nothing you can do.'
jokes.setup: Liz says 'you can't change New York' and invokes Jay-Z as authority
jokes.punchline: She misquotes 'Empire State of Mind' replacing 'jungle' with 'bunghole' and 'are made of' with 'are made up' — both changes subtly degrade the song and her credibility as a cultural authority
jokes.explanation: Outstanding. Two-level joke: the misquote makes thematic sense for Liz's pessimism ('bunghole' instead of 'jungle,' 'made up' instead of 'made of') while also being funny purely as a malapropism. Liz citing Jay-Z as if she knows the lyrics when she clearly doesn't is perfect character work. 'Bunghole' as a direct replacement for 'jungle' is inspired. One of the episode's best.

jokes.text: That's a wrap. That commercial parody is gonna be hilarious. What's a commercial?
jokes.setup: The commercial parody shoot wraps up
jokes.punchline: Tracy asks what a commercial is — suggesting he has been participating in something without any understanding of its basic premise
jokes.explanation: Classic Tracy moment. The timing is perfect — waiting until after the wrap to ask. His total disengagement from the reality of television (despite being a TV star) is well-established character comedy. Economy is excellent.

jokes.text: Hopefully it's not an important parg of my blurn.
jokes.setup: Liz is visibly sick; someone asks about her symptoms
jokes.punchline: Her illness has so addled her speech that 'part of my brain' comes out as 'parg of my blurn' — the malapropism itself demonstrates the condition she's describing
jokes.explanation: Self-demonstrating joke — Liz's illness is proven by the very words she uses to describe it. 'Parg of my blurn' is a well-crafted sick-speak approximation that sounds exactly right. The concept is clean and well-executed.

jokes.text: Paul's finally coming home tonight. And his sexpectations will be high.
jokes.setup: Jenna explains why she doesn't want to get sick
jokes.punchline: 'Sexpectations' as a portmanteau of 'sex' and 'expectations' is a Jenna-specific coinage that encapsulates her relationship priorities perfectly
jokes.explanation: Good portmanteau that works as natural Jenna dialogue. 'Sexpectations' feels like something she'd actually say without irony. Character integration is strong.

jokes.text: Maybe I should wear this home. Show Chris what he'll be looking at in 40 years. Looser skin, same underwear.
jokes.setup: Jenna is wearing the old-lady costume for the commercial parody
jokes.punchline: She considers wearing it home as a preview for her boyfriend — 'same underwear' implies she'll be wearing the same underwear in 40 years, a darkly specific detail about her continuity
jokes.explanation: 'Same underwear' is the unexpected button — it recontextualizes from vanity joke to a specific, slightly gross detail that makes it memorable. Good structure.

jokes.text: I can't order you a car unless it's after 9:00, or you have a note from your killer.
jokes.setup: Liz asks for a car home because she's old, sick, and there's a Monk rerun on
jokes.punchline: Pete gives two conditions for a car: after 9pm OR 'a note from your killer' — implying the latter is an equally standard bureaucratic exception
jokes.explanation: Excellent absurdist comedy. 'A note from your killer' treated as bureaucratic equivalence to a time-of-day rule is inspired. Pete's deadpan delivery of what is functionally an impossible condition as if it were routine policy is perfectly executed. Very quotable.

jokes.text: I have a criminal skull shape.
jokes.setup: Len the security guard sees Tracy with Jack and notes he'd jump to conclusions about Tracy
jokes.punchline: Tracy cheerfully self-identifies as having phrenologically suspicious features — embracing a pseudoscientific racist concept as self-description without irony
jokes.explanation: Tracy's self-aware-yet-oblivious delivery makes this land. The phrenology reference is an unexpected level of specificity. The economy is superb — four words carrying enormous character information.

jokes.text: Commissioner Kelly and I are friends. We have competing columns in Irish Arguments Weekly, America's only all-caps magazine.
jokes.setup: Jack name-drops his connection to the police commissioner
jokes.punchline: 'Irish Arguments Weekly' as a publication is funny on its own; 'America's only all-caps magazine' is an inspired specification that implies both the publication's angry tone and its niche ethnic-religious-combative identity
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest inventions. 'Irish Arguments Weekly' is funny. 'America's only all-caps magazine' adds a layer of specific absurdism that elevates it — the all-caps detail implies the magazine's entire editorial voice is one of aggravated shouting. Perfect Jack Donaghy worldbuilding.

jokes.text: I was part of a special task force of very young-looking cops who infiltrated high schools.
jokes.setup: Len mentions he was once a police officer
jokes.punchline: His specific detail — young-looking cops in high schools — directly references the premise of 21 Jump Street, implying Len is basically a real-life Jonah Hill character
jokes.explanation: The setup is good and the pop culture awareness is there. The joke requires the audience to connect the dots (21 Jump Street) which most comedy-savvy viewers will.

jokes.text: I'm not embarrassed. I get all my outfits at Ann Taylor Loft. Their clothes fit my body and my budget.
jokes.setup: Jack notices Len's suit and implies it's beneath his station
jokes.punchline: Len's defensive pride in Ann Taylor Loft — delivered unprompted with brand loyalty — reveals his modest financial situation while functioning as an inadvertent advertisement
jokes.explanation: The specificity of Ann Taylor Loft is funny — it's a real, decidedly un-Jack brand. 'Fit my body and my budget' is a good, slightly sad line. Works well in establishing Len as a character.

jokes.text: What do you make? 40 grand a year. But don't let the woman who's blackmailing me know that.
jokes.setup: Jack pressures Len for salary information to prove his point about class
jokes.punchline: Len reveals his salary then immediately warns Jack not to tell the woman blackmailing him — delivered as if this is a routine concern everyone has
jokes.explanation: The blackmail detail is thrown in with complete casualness, as if it's the most normal thing in the world. The contrast between the mundane salary figure and the extreme personal circumstance is excellent. Good dark comedy with perfect economy.

jokes.text: Despite the hundreds of dollars I pay every year in taxes.
jokes.setup: Jack complains that the police won't help him despite his contributions
jokes.punchline: A man of Jack's wealth pays 'hundreds of dollars' in taxes — implying he pays essentially nothing relative to his income through aggressive tax avoidance
jokes.explanation: Excellent satirical joke delivered perfectly in character. Jack's pride in paying 'hundreds' of dollars while being obscenely wealthy is both character comedy and sharp political satire. The understatement does all the work. Very quotable.

jokes.text: No, if I sneeze, I'll do it like the president taught me. [Liz demonstrating the sneeze technique]
jokes.setup: Earlier Liz complained no one watched Obama's sneeze press conference
jokes.punchline: Now sick and about to sneeze, she actually performs the presidential sneeze technique — presumably some awkward elbow-into-face maneuver — the callback pays off visually
jokes.explanation: Good callback payoff. Liz's rule-following vindicated in real time — she actually does the thing she judged others for not doing. The physical comedy is inferred but the character integrity of the moment is strong.

jokes.text: I'm pregnant with a kitty cat.
jokes.setup: Liz is visibly ill and making sick noises; this appears to be mid-sneeze or illness symptom sequence
jokes.punchline: Non-sequitur declaration while ill — possibly a fever dream or just illness-addled nonsense delivered with complete sincerity
jokes.explanation: Funny in isolation as pure absurdism but doesn't have much structure to it — it's funny because it's random and specific ('kitty cat' rather than just 'cat'). Works more on delivery than craft.

jokes.text: Those are my popsicles!
jokes.setup: Liz is in the midst of her illness episode
jokes.punchline: Another non-sequitur outburst — presumably hallucinating or dreaming — the specificity of 'my popsicles' being her fevered concern is very Liz
jokes.explanation: The food-possessiveness is very Liz Lemon, which gives it some character grounding. But structurally it's just a random outburst — funny but not sophisticated.

jokes.text: I'm wearing an edible nightgown. It's breadstick flavor and it comes with a dipping sauce.
jokes.setup: Jenna greets Paul seductively after his return
jokes.punchline: An edible nightgown is already a joke; specifying 'breadstick flavor' with a dipping sauce makes it simultaneously more specific and more absurd — the food/sex combination is peak Jenna/Paul
jokes.explanation: Exceptional Jenna joke. The escalation from 'edible nightgown' (already absurd) to 'breadstick flavor' to 'comes with a dipping sauce' is perfectly structured escalation. The food specificity (breadstick, not something romantic) makes it funnier — this is a practical, Italian-restaurant-themed sex garment. Only Jenna.

jokes.text: Uh-oh, yawns are contagious. Like all the Thai STDs my penis is about to give you.
jokes.setup: Paul yawns after arriving home and Jenna yawns too
jokes.punchline: Paul notes yawns are contagious, then extends the contagion metaphor to the STDs he's apparently contracted during his travels — delivered as romantic foreplay
jokes.explanation: Superb structure. The setup uses the yawn-contagion scientific fact to pivot to something completely unexpected — STD disclosure as romantic anticipation. 'Thai STDs my penis is about to give you' is so specific and so casually delivered that it's genuinely shocking-funny. The character integration is excellent — this is exactly the Jenna/Paul dynamic.

jokes.text: The sex monkey I bought in Jakarta.
jokes.setup: Paul says he's going to unpack — the audience expects clothes or gifts
jokes.punchline: He's unpacking a sex monkey from Jakarta — an object so specific and so wrong on multiple levels that the gap from expectation to reality is enormous
jokes.explanation: Excellent escalation of the Jenna/Paul perversity. The specificity of 'Jakarta' makes the monkey geographically situated, implying Paul went to Southeast Asia specifically for this. Five words that contain an entire depraved story. The economy is remarkable.

jokes.text: Did we mix up our days and accidentally both roofie each other? Or did we just fall asleep? What, like some boring, normal, sit-com couple? Like Mr. Brady and Tiger the dog?
jokes.setup: Jenna and Paul realize they just fell asleep together without doing anything sexual
jokes.punchline: Jenna lists possible explanations — mutual roofie-ing first — then the mundane explanation (falling asleep) treated as equally unbelievable. The comparison to 'Mr. Brady and Tiger the dog' is a bizarrely specific Brady Bunch reference that underscores her unfamiliarity with normal couplehood
jokes.explanation: Multi-layered excellence. 'Accidentally both roofie each other' as the first hypothesis is a perfect Jenna/Paul joke — for them this is more plausible than just falling asleep. The meta-sitcom reference ('sit-com couple') from a character ON a sitcom is great. 'Mr. Brady and Tiger the dog' as the example of normal couple behavior is inexplicably specific and funnier for it.

jokes.text: It's a whole new fetish called... Normalling.
jokes.setup: Jenna and Paul reframe their mundane night together as kinky rather than admitting they're becoming a normal couple
jokes.punchline: 'Normalling' — treating ordinary domestic behavior as a sexual fetish — is a perfect encapsulation of their characters' pathological need to make everything transgressive
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and a top-tier 30 Rock concept. 'Normalling' as a coined fetish term is brilliantly economical — one word that captures the entire thematic arc of the Jenna/Paul subplot. The joke works because it's both character-specific (only they would do this) and conceptually sharp (it inverts fetish logic). The episode commits to the bit fully, which earns it.

jokes.text: And I put that Afghan all over you because I thought your feet might get chilly. So chilly.
jokes.setup: Paul confesses his own normalling act — covering Jenna with a blanket
jokes.punchline: 'So chilly' appended after — he's applying the language of sexual response to foot temperature, treating 'chilly' as a trigger word in the normalling framework
jokes.explanation: The 'so chilly' echo of Jenna's 'sick bitch' energy is perfectly calibrated. Paul turns foot temperature into erotic language. The economy of 'so chilly' doing all that work is impressive. Great running gag development.

jokes.text: We go out as a couple to Bed Bath and Beyond and shop for home necessities. In front of everybody.
jokes.setup: Jenna and Paul escalate their normalling plans
jokes.punchline: 'In front of everybody' — as if shopping at Bed Bath and Beyond is a public sex act — implies they're planning to normalize in public as exhibitionists would
jokes.explanation: The escalation of normalling into public normalling is perfect. 'In front of everybody' recontextualizes a completely innocent activity as transgressive exhibitionism. Bed Bath and Beyond as the venue of choice is specifically, perfectly mundane. One of the normalling subplot's best beats.

jokes.text: Normalling in public? You delicious whore.
jokes.setup: Jenna proposes normalling in public at Bed Bath and Beyond
jokes.punchline: Paul's reaction — 'You delicious whore' — applies the language of sexual admiration to Jenna's suggestion of domestic shopping, perfectly extending the normalling logic
jokes.explanation: Perfect button on the Bed Bath & Beyond exchange. 'You delicious whore' as a response to 'let's go to Bed Bath & Beyond' is an inspired juxtaposition. The economy is excellent and the character voice is completely consistent.

jokes.text: Really, Trump? My idea is stupid? Well, you make your hair every morning by sticking your head in a cotton candy machine.
jokes.setup: Jack is apparently on the phone with Donald Trump, pitching his private police department idea
jokes.punchline: Trump has criticized Jack's idea — Jack retorts by roasting Trump's hair, comparing it to cotton candy machine output, which is both accurate and devastating
jokes.explanation: Good Trump hair joke — the cotton candy machine specificity is better than a generic 'your hair is bad' insult. The context (Trump calling Jack's idea stupid while Jack is forming a private police force) is rich dramatic irony. Slight deduction for Trump jokes being ubiquitous even in 2012.

jokes.text: Even Tommy Hilfiger turned me down, and you'd think that he, of all people, would understand the lower classes can ruin something.
jokes.setup: Jack is recruiting wealthy allies for his private police force
jokes.punchline: The implication is that Tommy Hilfiger (whose brand was allegedly ruined when embraced by hip-hop/street culture in the 90s, per an urban legend) would sympathize with Jack's anti-lower-class agenda — a darkly pointed joke about fashion brand anxiety
jokes.explanation: Sharp cultural-historical joke that requires some knowledge of the Tommy Hilfiger brand mythology but rewards those who have it. Jack's logic is twisted but internally consistent — and the implication that Hilfiger would be a natural ally in class warfare is darkly funny satire of fashion's racial anxieties.

jokes.text: Plaxico Burress just called our idea 'poorly thought out'. Then hung up by shooting his own phone.
jokes.setup: Jack's private police force is getting rejected by wealthy contacts
jokes.punchline: Plaxico Burress — the NFL player who accidentally shot himself in a nightclub — hung up on them by literally shooting his phone, consistent with his established history of accidental self-shooting
jokes.explanation: Exceptional joke. The structure is perfect: Plaxico's criticism first, then the method of hanging up that reveals everything about the character without stating it. 'Shooting his own phone' as a logical extension of Burress's real-world incident is brilliant economy. The joke trusts the audience completely. One of the episode's best.

jokes.text: Did anyone cheer me, or name a sandwich after me that would maybe be Turkey, pastrami, Swiss, Russian dressing, Cole slaw and potato chips?
jokes.setup: Liz recounts how she used to try to enforce NYC rules and got nothing in return
jokes.punchline: Her vision of civic reward is not a plaque or a medal but a very specific sandwich — and she's clearly already designed it in her head
jokes.explanation: Near-perfect character comedy. The sandwich is so specific (six ingredients, each chosen deliberately) that it's clear Liz has genuinely imagined this as her ideal civic tribute. Turkey, pastrami, Swiss, Russian dressing, coleslaw AND potato chips — the chips inside the sandwich are peak Liz. This could only be Liz Lemon. Character integration is exceptional.

jokes.text: Yes, a native American paradise! [In response to Jack saying 'New York was once great']
jokes.setup: Jack talks about New York's former greatness and needing to restore it
jokes.punchline: Liz interprets 'what New York once was' literally — before European settlement — deflating Jack's romanticism with historical reality
jokes.explanation: Good interruption joke. Liz's literal-minded response to Jack's rhetoric lands as a well-timed deflation. The historical accuracy makes the irony pointed.

jokes.text: Anyhoo, Tracy, in the dog boner sketch.
jokes.setup: Jack has just delivered a stirring speech about leading New York to greatness — rising rhetoric about beacons and justice
jokes.punchline: Liz immediately undercuts the speech by pivoting to work business involving a 'dog boner sketch' — the tonal whiplash is enormous
jokes.explanation: Great tonal whiplash. The contrast between Jack's soaring civic rhetoric and 'dog boner sketch' is maximum. 'Anyhoo' as the transition word is perfect — it's Liz's most efficient meeting-redirect sound. The specific content of the sketch she's pivoting to (dog boners) earns its own laugh.

jokes.text: I hereby officially announce my candidacy for the office of Mayor of the city of New York. Vote for Jack Donaghy. Slogan to come.
jokes.setup: Jack has delivered a stirring speech about leading New York — it sounds like a political announcement
jokes.punchline: 'Slogan to come' — Jack is so committed to the mayoral announcement theater that he formally notes his slogan isn't ready yet, as if this is part of the official announcement
jokes.explanation: 'Slogan to come' is the perfect button. The formal structure of a political announcement (complete with voting instruction) ending with the admission that a basic element isn't ready yet shows Jack's impulse control trumping his preparation. Very in character.

jokes.text: You know if we got cloth place mats then we could just throw them in the laundry. Well, these vinyl ones say dishwasher safe, that's easy. Yeah, easy for the person who never does the dishes.
jokes.setup: Jenna and Paul are normalling at Bed Bath and Beyond
jokes.punchline: They are having a completely mundane domestic disagreement about placemats — argued with the earnestness of a long-married couple — and Jenna's passive-aggressive 'easy for the person who never does the dishes' is a perfect recreation of normal couple fighting
jokes.explanation: The normalling payoff is excellent. The placemat debate is so perfectly mundane, and Jenna's passive-aggression about dishes is exactly the kind of petty couple dynamic they're fetishizing. The comedy comes from the commitment — this is genuinely realistic domestic bickering, which is funny because of who's doing it.

jokes.text: What we're doing is so sick, right? How many times have you climaxed? Zero. Me too. Bathroom organizers! Oh!
jokes.setup: Jenna and Paul continue shopping at Bed Bath and Beyond as their normalling fetish
jokes.punchline: They're checking in on their arousal levels, which are zero — then have a synchronized orgasmic reaction to bathroom organizers
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's absolute best moments. The structure is perfect: establish zero climaxes (anticlimax), then immediate reversal when they discover bathroom organizers. The orgasmic 'Oh!' over home organization products is a perfect 30 Rock escalation that simultaneously mocks the normalling concept and delivers on it. 'How many times have you climaxed? Zero. Me too.' is a brutally funny exchange. This is exceptional writing.

jokes.text: Do you know anyone who wants to be called Daryl Weenus?
jokes.setup: Tracy announces he got a list of voter names for Jack's campaign
jokes.punchline: The only example he provides is 'Daryl Weenus' — either the list is fake, Tracy made it up, or this is a real registered voter's name
jokes.explanation: 'Daryl Weenus' is a perfectly chosen fake-sounding name — 'Daryl' is plausibly real, 'Weenus' is anatomical slang. The combination is funny. The setup of Tracy having 'a huge list' only to produce this one example is good structural comedy.

jokes.text: I just registered the domain name for my campaign website... Jack-Donaghy-is-running-for-mayor-2013-new-York-this-is-the-website.com. That's as close as I could get. Everything else was already pornography.
jokes.setup: Jack is building his mayoral campaign infrastructure
jokes.punchline: The domain name is absurdly long and literal; the explanation that every shorter variation was already taken by pornographic sites is a perfect indictment of early internet domain squatting
jokes.explanation: The domain name joke is well-constructed — the name itself is funny as a run-on, and 'everything else was already pornography' is both a true observation about early 2010s internet and a perfect button. Jack's casual delivery of an insanely long URL is good character comedy.

jokes.text: I also got you these goofy water balloons my mom's friend Ron used to always send me out to buy.
jokes.setup: Kenneth lists items he got for Jack including 'goofy water balloons'
jokes.punchline: The audience immediately understands 'goofy water balloons' are condoms; Kenneth does not. 'Mom's friend Ron' as the adult who exploited Kenneth's innocence adds a layer of dark subtext
jokes.explanation: Classic Kenneth innocence joke elevated by the 'mom's friend Ron' detail — the implication that a sketchy adult figure regularly sent young Kenneth out to buy condoms while not explaining what they were is darker than the show typically goes. The misdirection works because we hear 'water balloons' and then put it together exactly as Jack does.

jokes.text: Thank you, Kenneth. I know they're condoms.
jokes.setup: Kenneth presents the 'goofy water balloons' to Jack
jokes.punchline: Jack's flat acknowledgment that he knows what they are — without any further reaction or judgment — is perfectly in character and delivers the joke's punchline with maximum economy
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy joke. Four words — 'I know they're condoms' — land the punchline for joke 64 with complete deadpan authority. Jack doesn't explain, doesn't react emotionally, just states the fact. The brevity IS the joke.

jokes.text: Hang on... have you not left this building since you were mugged?
jokes.setup: Jack reveals he's been stockpiling supplies to never leave his office
jokes.punchline: Tracy — whose own relationship with reality is tenuous — is the one noticing Jack's avoidance behavior, which is a funny inversion (the least reliable person in the room being the reality check)
jokes.explanation: The comedic value is in the role reversal — Tracy as the grounded one — which is established characterization. The joke is in the dramatic irony more than the line itself.

jokes.text: All I had was a Chewbacca costume made out of used hair extensions.
jokes.setup: Tracy tells Jack about hiding after his first mugging and what made him feel safe
jokes.punchline: The specific material of the Chewbacca costume — used hair extensions — implies Tracy sourced them second-hand, which raises infinite questions about origin and hygiene
jokes.explanation: Very strong Tracy absurdism grounded in specific, tactile detail. 'Used hair extensions' transforms a Chewbacca costume from silly to specifically Tracy-gross. The implication that this made him feel 'invincible' is perfect character logic. High character integration.

jokes.text: Perfectly-executed Chewbacca sounds! [Tracy makes Chewbacca noises to demonstrate]
jokes.setup: Tracy explains the Chewbacca costume made him feel invincible like someone who wouldn't freeze when mugged
jokes.punchline: He spontaneously performs a Chewbacca roar mid-story, presumably to demonstrate the costume's powers, then the show labels it 'perfectly-executed' through dialogue or reaction
jokes.explanation: Physical comedy that earns its place through Tracy's commitment. The self-description 'perfectly-executed' is funny meta-commentary on his own performance. Works best visually.

jokes.text: Then I'm gonna say to you what I say to all my sharks right before they die. Let's go outside.
jokes.setup: Tracy encourages Jack to face his fear and go outside
jokes.punchline: Tracy apparently keeps sharks that die regularly, and his pre-death send-off speech to them is 'let's go outside' — implying either he takes dying sharks outside, or this is what he says to encourage creatures before their end
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's absolute best lines. The joke contains an entire absurd world in one sentence: Tracy has sharks (plural), they die regularly enough to warrant a ritual speech, and his ritual speech is one of the most mundane possible phrases. The delivery as encouragement to Jack makes 'let's go outside' simultaneously threatening and inspiring. This is 30 Rock at its finest — maximum information, maximum absurdism, maximum economy.

jokes.text: Oh, Jenna, I have a friend... / Yeah, well I have a million friends. I get so many birthday cards it's embarrassing.
jokes.setup: Pete begins to tell Jenna about a friend with an idea.
jokes.punchline: Jenna immediately interrupts to assert her social dominance by claiming a million friends — the specific detail of birthday cards being 'embarrassing' implies it's embarrassing how many she gets (not that she's embarrassed for having them).
jokes.explanation: Good character comedy for Jenna — her narcissistic non-sequitur derails Pete's sentence. The birthday cards detail is funny in its specificity. Slightly weaker because it's mostly setup for the Normalling reveal to follow.

jokes.text: This is normalling. It's a weird sex thing. Paul and I do things like reboot the Internet... and discuss whether the chair would be better over by the window where there's more light?
jokes.setup: Liz explains normalling to Pete; Pete starts completing the mundane examples himself
jokes.punchline: Pete inadvertently knows exactly what normalling looks like because he just describes his own life — the punchline is that Pete's marriage IS normalling without the fetish framing
jokes.explanation: Smart structural joke. Pete's involuntary participation — completing Liz's description of normalling activities — reveals that his own marriage is what Jenna and Paul are fetishizing. The comedy of recognition is strong here. 'That's just couple stuff' lands as both a punchline and a reveal.

jokes.text: Hey, you and Paul should come by the house sometime. We'll have dinner, play Scattergories.
jokes.setup: Pete realizes Jenna and Paul's normalling is just normal couple stuff
jokes.punchline: Pete immediately invites them to his house for dinner and Scattergories — the most aggressively normal couple activity — completely unaware this would be the ultimate normalling destination for Jenna and Paul
jokes.explanation: Good extension of the running gag. Pete doesn't realize he's offering Jenna and Paul their sexual fantasy. 'Scattergories' as the specific game chosen is a funny touch — not even a cool board game.

jokes.text: Oh, you smell like when the Stone Mountain tire fire joined up with the corpse fire, and then swept through the downtown manure district. It was our fault for letting those high schoolers dance at their prom.
jokes.setup: Kenneth reacts to Liz's gym bag smell
jokes.punchline: Kenneth describes the smell through a geological narrative of converging fire disasters, adding 'manure district' as if it's a real neighborhood, then pivots to blaming a high school prom — implying Stone Mountain has multiple fire zones AND a controversial prom history
jokes.explanation: Exceptional Kenneth absurdism rooted in his Southern background. The structure escalates beautifully: tire fire → corpse fire → manure district → high school prom guilt. Each element adds a new dimension of awful. 'The downtown manure district' is an inspired construction. The prom detail implies a small-town gothic backstory for Kenneth. One of his best moments.

jokes.text: I'm gonna clear out that whole theater and watch a sneak peek of The Hunger Games by myself. It'll be my greatest triumph. There's a Q&A afterwards with... eh, the screenwriter? Bleh.
jokes.setup: Liz plans to use her terrible smell to empty a movie theater
jokes.punchline: She's excited about Hunger Games but dismisses the screenwriter Q&A with 'bleh' — a very specific hierarchy of what's worth experiencing
jokes.explanation: The 'eh, the screenwriter? Bleh' button is the funniest part — Liz's value system where a screenwriter Q&A is actively worse than nothing is very her. Good character moment.

jokes.text: Plastic cups go on the top rack of the dishwasher so they don't melt. Otherwise, no rules.
jokes.setup: Kenneth urges Liz to remember her rule-following self; she dramatically declares 'no rules'
jokes.punchline: She can't commit to full anarchy — she must carve out one specific dishwasher rule as the bedrock of civilization, then immediately declares no other rules exist
jokes.explanation: The episode's single best joke. Perfect structure, perfect character integration, perfect economy. The joke works because it's completely true to Liz Lemon: she cannot actually abandon all rules because the dishwasher rack rule is genuinely important to her — but she frames it as the one exception to her new anarchic philosophy. 'Otherwise, no rules' after specifying the one rule that matters most is brilliant. This could ONLY be Liz Lemon. Extremely quotable and gets funnier on rewatch as you appreciate how precisely it captures her character.

jokes.text: Well, well, well. If it isn't the tuxedo himself. Shouldn't you be outside, fixing the city?
jokes.setup: Liz (now in full disgusting-smell mode) encounters Jack, who has been hiding in his office
jokes.punchline: Liz calls Jack 'the tuxedo himself' — referencing the episode's title and Jack's armor — while she is equally hiding from the world in her own armor (the smell)
jokes.explanation: Good scene-setting dialogue that draws the parallel between Jack's tuxedo-as-armor and Liz's smell-as-armor. The title callback is earned. Works more as plot than comedy but has comedic elements.

jokes.text: Well, you look even closer to death than usual. What happened to you? Are you scared? The back of the 'B' train certainly was. I had the whole car to myself.
jokes.setup: Jack and Liz are both projecting strength while hiding; they trade insults
jokes.punchline: Liz reveals she cleared a subway car with her smell — meant as a power move — while Jack notes she looks near death, deflating her bravado
jokes.explanation: Solid banter exchange. 'Closer to death than usual' is a good Jack line. 'The back of the B train certainly was' is a nice inversion — Liz treating the train's reaction as a conquest. Good but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Is that your gym bag? Aren't you a human woman? It's these new microfibers. They keep you dry but it all has to go somewhere.
jokes.setup: Jack is appalled by Liz's gym bag smell
jokes.punchline: Liz's explanation — that moisture-wicking technology simply relocates the sweat rather than eliminating it — is delivered as a quasi-scientific defense that's both funny and disturbingly logical
jokes.explanation: The microfiber explanation is actually a funny piece of observational comedy with a grain of truth — the idea that performance fabric doesn't eliminate sweat but concentrates it is gross and plausible. 'Aren't you a human woman?' is a great Jack line.

jokes.text: I've always wanted to say that, and I can't believe I've wasted it on you.
jokes.setup: Jack delivers a dramatic 'there's a war out there and you're gonna have to pick a side' speech to Liz
jokes.punchline: He immediately regrets using the line on Liz — apparently saving it for a more worthy dramatic occasion — undermining his own moment of gravitas
jokes.explanation: Excellent meta-comedy about performative drama. Jack has been collecting dramatic lines for special occasions and is genuinely disappointed Liz prompted this one. The self-awareness immediately deflates his own speech. Perfect economy and character integration — this is Jack's relationship with his own persona laid bare.

jokes.text: The old Liz would have agreed with you. But that was two days ago. Now, I don't cross lines, I just make 'em... disappear.
jokes.setup: Jack says someone's gonna stop Liz's selfish behavior; New York will stop her
jokes.punchline: Liz's dramatic declaration of her new philosophy — 'that was two days ago' deflates any gravitas, since her 'transformation' happened roughly 48 hours prior
jokes.explanation: 'That was two days ago' is an excellent deflation of Liz's attempted villain arc. She's trying to be mysterious and edgy about a two-day behavior change. The bathrobe-level danger of her 'dark side' is captured perfectly.

jokes.text: But if Daryl Weenus is right, if we're just a couple, why don't we hate it?
jokes.setup: Jenna and Paul have a serious conversation about whether normalling is a fetish or just their relationship evolving
jokes.punchline: She cites 'Daryl Weenus' as a philosophical authority on couples — the absurd name treated with complete earnestness elevates it
jokes.explanation: Good callback that gives the 'Daryl Weenus' name additional comedic life. The name treated as a wise philosopher is funny.

jokes.text: I always imagined this kind of thing would make me wanna tear my hair out and rip my skin off. But with you, it feels as natural as... having someone tear your hair out and rip your skin off.
jokes.setup: Paul is trying to express that normalling feels natural and good
jokes.punchline: His analogy for 'natural' bottoms out at 'having someone tear your hair out and rip your skin off' — which reveals his baseline is violent body horror, making domesticity remarkable by comparison
jokes.explanation: Exceptional structure. The misdirection is perfect: he sets up a simile about naturalness and lands on something that would be described as torture. The logic is flawless within the Jenna/Paul universe — of course their 'natural' feeling is referenced against violence. The structure (expectation → exact repetition of what he rejected) is very well constructed.

jokes.text: We spend the next three months alone, doing every depraved thing we can think of with as many people as we can and if this, right now, is still the happiest we can make ourselves, we'll stay together forever.
jokes.setup: Paul explains what a 'sexual walkabout' entails
jokes.punchline: The proposal is actually oddly romantic — they're conducting a scientific experiment in hedonism to confirm their love, which is the most Jenna/Paul possible approach to commitment
jokes.explanation: Good joke that works more as character revelation than pure comedy. The internal logic of the walkabout as a fidelity test is surprisingly sound, which makes it funnier.

jokes.text: Gym bag, check. Tupperware vat of steamed broccoli, check. Talking to myself to seem crazy... moo-goo!
jokes.setup: Liz is preparing her subway armor for public transit
jokes.punchline: She has a checklist including 'talking to myself to seem crazy' — then immediately performs a crazy person sound ('moo-goo!') as a test run, which is itself a form of the thing being described
jokes.explanation: Excellent meta-joke. Liz has a deliberate arsenal of antisocial behaviors and is running through a checklist. 'Moo-goo' as her chosen crazy-person sound is inspired specificity — not a generic crazy word, but 'moo-goo,' which sounds vaguely like Chinese food (moo goo gai pan) and is nonsensical enough to work. The self-consciousness of the performance is perfect Liz.

jokes.text: You've skied Mount St. Helens, made eye contact with Michelle Bachmann, been trapped under a Boulder for 128 hours. You're not scared of anything.
jokes.setup: Jack gives himself a pep talk before going outside
jokes.punchline: He lists accomplishments to prove his bravery: Mount St. Helens skiing and being trapped under a boulder are extreme; 'made eye contact with Michelle Bachmann' is listed between them as equally terrifying, which is the punchline
jokes.explanation: Strong list joke with excellent construction. The reference to 127 Hours (trapped under boulder for 128 hours — one hour longer, because Jack is more extreme) adds a layer. 'Made eye contact with Michelle Bachmann' sandwiched between physical extremes as an equal danger is sharp political comedy. The 128 vs 127 detail is a nice touch.

jokes.text: Gimme $20!
jokes.setup: Jack has finally ventured outside; Liz is prepared with her scary subway armor (smell, broccoli, crazy talk)
jokes.punchline: The tense confrontation reveals it's Liz — who was trying to get movie money — and she mugs Jack in her terrifying persona, completing the episode's thematic circle of the rules-follower becoming a criminal
jokes.explanation: Good structural payoff. Liz has become Jack's mugger — the episode's arcs (Jack's tuxedo armor, Liz's selfishness) collide. The economy of 'Gimme $20' as the confrontation line is excellent.

jokes.text: You caught that lunatic that's been terrorizing the subway. The worst criminal in #N-Y-C.
jokes.setup: Jack throws Liz into the garbage, thinking she's a criminal; bystanders cheer
jokes.punchline: The crowd cheers Jack for catching 'the worst criminal in NYC' — who is actually Liz, a middle-class TV writer who wanted movie money — satirizing how crime narratives work
jokes.explanation: Good satirical payoff. The crowd's reaction validates the episode's social commentary — they've caught 'the worst criminal' who is Liz Lemon. The song lyric format ('The worst criminal in #N-Y-C') implies this is how the bystanders' cheers sound.

jokes.text: You're the only woman I could ever fight to regain my manhood.
jokes.setup: Jack and Liz have a moment of connection after the confrontation
jokes.punchline: Jack's compliment to Liz is phrased as a romantic acknowledgment but the content is specifically about her role as the person he'd physically fight for ego restoration — a backhanded compliment only Jack could deliver
jokes.explanation: Beautiful character comedy. The line reads as tender but is deeply specific in a Jack way — his 'manhood' needed restoration and Liz was instrumental. The phrasing ('ever fight') implies he's considered many women for this role. Very quotable and character-specific.

jokes.text: They're cheering you for stopping me. Old Liz was right. People do want rules!
jokes.setup: The crowd cheers Jack for stopping the 'criminal'
jokes.punchline: Liz, while being thrown in garbage, has an epiphany — the crowd's reaction proves her original philosophy correct, completed while she's literally in a trash pile
jokes.explanation: Good thematic payoff delivered with appropriate irony. 'Old Liz was right' is a funny acknowledgment that her 'dark period' lasted roughly 36 hours. The revelation happening from inside a garbage pile is fitting.

jokes.text: So, are you still running for mayor? The city no longer needs me. For now.
jokes.setup: The crisis is resolved; Jack has reclaimed his sense of self
jokes.punchline: 'For now' — Jack immediately hedges his graceful exit with an implication he'll be back to the mayoral ambition at any moment
jokes.explanation: 'For now' as a two-word button is economically excellent. It's both a character moment (Jack's ego) and a structural joke (the setup was long; the punchline is tiny). Very in character.

jokes.text: Reminds me of us. I'll never forget the first time you dressed up like an old lady and I threw you into some garbage.
jokes.setup: Jack and Liz share a moment that apparently echoes earlier in their relationship
jokes.punchline: Jack's romantic nostalgia is for the time he threw Liz into garbage — treating a violent act as a sweet memory, completely in character for their relationship
jokes.explanation: Beautiful character comedy. Jack's version of romantic reminiscence involves throwing people into garbage. The framing of the episode's events as a new 'first time' for their relationship is tender in a very 30 Rock way. High character integration and quotability.

jokes.text: Good-bye, my love. For now.
jokes.setup: Jack and Liz part ways.
jokes.punchline: 'For now' — the same qualifier from his mayoral withdrawal — applied to his relationship with Liz, collapsing the political and personal in one small phrase.
jokes.explanation: A satisfying callback that doubles the meaning of 'for now' — city and Liz simultaneously. The economy is exceptional: five words resolve both the episode's plot and the Jack/Liz dynamic. Sweet without being saccharine.

jokes.text: New York City. Villains and heroes. The 1% and the 99. 8 million people in this crazy, beautiful city, and I, Jenna Maroney, am going to go to town on every last one of them.
jokes.setup: The episode closes with a romantic monologue about New York City — the structure mirrors the episode's opening debate about the city
jokes.punchline: The monologue sounds like a heroic declaration about civic love, but 'go to town on every last one of them' in Jenna's mouth is clearly about her sexual walkabout — she's doing the city
jokes.explanation: Excellent closing joke. The structure mirrors a prestige TV city-love monologue but the punchline reveals Jenna is announcing her sexual walkabout to the city at large. 'Go to town on every last one of them' is perfectly ambiguous — noble civic purpose and licentious promise simultaneously. Very high character integration. Strong ending.

tmdb_overview: Fed up with New York City after being mugged, Jack sets out to protect the safety of the city's elite by announcing his run for mayor. Meanwhile, Liz revels in sacrificing the good of the city to look out for her own interests, and Jenna and Paul are thrilled by the perversion of acting like a normal couple.
insight: Absurdist momentum drives 73 jokes in 23 minutes—nearly triple the show's baseline density.
